newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Swiss unemployment hits post-war high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss unemployment hits post-war high.

text.p: Switzerland reported a record high jobless rate on Thursday and a less than optimistic outlook in the latest dismal data highlighting its need for more structural change and a reversal of its protectionist mentality.
Unemployment rose to 5.3 percent in December from 5.1 percent the previous month, the highest monthly rate since World War Two, the Swiss Office of Trade, Industry and Labour said.
The average jobless rate rose to 4.7 percent for all of 1996 and was likely to rise further in 1997, the office also said.

"Even if a stabilising of the unemployment numbers, or even a slight decline comes in the spring and in the summer, the average joblessness level will be between 15,000 and 20,000 higher than last year before we can anticipate a slight decline in 1998," the office said in a statement released in Berne.
The December rate was marginally higher than expected.
"They (the data) are slightly higher than we had forecast, but are in line with our general trend," Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) economist Manfred Gutmann said.
UBS had forecast a 5.2 percent December unemployment rate.
In addition, the statistics office reported that retail sales in November fell 0.8 percent.
The Centre for Economic Activity said its economic barometer rose by only 0.1 percent in November and that an improvement in the first few months of 1997 was not to be expected.
Gutmann said the jobless rise in December may have been due, at least in part, to a decline in construction activity caused by the extremely cold weather during the month.
But Swiss economic recovery has been hampered for some time by the weak economies of its main trading partners, especially in Europe.

Perhaps just as detrimental, the economists say, are the protectionist attitudes and cartel-like business practices among all but the largest Swiss multi-national corporations -- structural deficiencies which have only now been brought to centre stage by the economy's anaemia.
"The domestic economy has been protected by cartels and has been closed to the rest of Europe," Credit Suisse Research economist Hilda Phan-Huy said.
A quarterly consensus of economic forecasts published in December put 1997 growth at 0.6 percent. The economy is widely estimated to have contracted by 0.75 percent last year.
Swiss growth has been near zero on average since 1990.
"In my view it's a problem of structural change in the Swiss economy," Gutmann said.
The prolonged economic weakness and a long-term outlook for only modest recovery at best is also keeping the Swiss franc and central bank monetary policy in focus.
Keeping the franc weak against major currencies such as the dollar and the mark has helped to boost Swiss exports.
The central bank has for some time kept downward pressure on money market rates with a view to helping the economy.
Money market dealers said the unemployment data did not provide any new clues to Swiss National Bank monetary policy, but all indications still pointed to interest rates staying low.
"The figures confirm what interest rates should be doing," one dealer said.

But uncertainties tied to Europe's adoption of a single currency could override expansive monetary policy and push the franc higher, putting renewed exchange rate pressures on Switzerland's export sector.
